q: Which responses are BLOCKS to therapeutic communication? (Select 3)

Keep the heaviest part of the load close to your body
Push wheeled equipment rather than pull it
Twist at the waist to turn with a load
Bend at the waist to pick something up
Pull the gurney along behind you

Together, toes touching, weight on your heels
Shoulder-width plus 12 inches, knees locked
One directly in front of the other, like walking

q: An inversion recovery sequence with a short TI of about 150–175 ms (at 1.5 T) is used to:
options: Null the signal from fat (STIR)
Null the signal from CSF (FLAIR)
Make the image T1 weighted with gadolinium
Reduce scan time
explain: After a 180° inversion, each tissue crosses zero at its own null point (TI ≈ 0.69 × T1). Fat has a very short T1, so its null is around 150–175 ms: STIR. CSF has a very long T1, so nulling it takes a long TI (about 2000+ ms): FLAIR.

q: Why does T2* decay happen faster than true T2 decay?
options: Magnetic field inhomogeneities add extra dephasing on top of spin-spin interactions
T2* uses a 180° refocusing pulse that speeds up the loss of transverse signal
T2* only measures fat, which loses its signal faster than water does
T2* is always measured in a stronger field, which shortens every relaxation time
explain: T2* = spin-spin dephasing PLUS dephasing from field inhomogeneities and susceptibility, so it decays faster. A spin echo's 180° pulse refocuses the inhomogeneity part, recovering true T2. Gradient echo (no 180°) gives T2*.

q: On a sagittal cervical spine, a thin bright line in the cord mimics a syrinx. This is likely:
options: Gibbs (truncation) artifact; increase the matrix and confirm on axial
Cross-talk between slices; increase the slice gap and repeat it
Chemical shift artifact; swap the phase and frequency directions
Zipper artifact from RF leakage; stop and call field service
explain: Gibbs/truncation artifact happens at sharp high-contrast edges (CSF and cord) when there are too few phase steps. Increase the matrix (more phase encodings) and check on axial images; a real syrinx will still be there.

q: To reduce swallowing motion artifact on a sagittal cervical spine:
options: Place a spatial saturation band over the tongue and epiglottis (anterior)
Increase NEX to 6 so the motion averages out across the acquisitions
Switch the phase direction to superior-inferior on the sagittal images
Use a longer TE so the swallowing motion has time to settle down
